items.label: section_header
items.text: 21 REVERSIBLE REACTIONS AND EQUILIBRIA

items.label: text
items.text: This chapter explores the idea of 'reversibility' in a reaction, and how you can control the conditions of such reactions in order to obtain as much as possible of what you want.

items.label: section_header
items.text: LEARNING OBJECTIVES

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know that some reactions are reversible and that this is indicated by the symbol ⇒ in equations

items.label: list_item
items.text: Describe reversible reactions such as the dehydration of hydrated copper(ll) sulfate and the effect of heat on ammonium chloride

items.label: section_header
items.text: CHEMISTRY ONLY

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know that a reversible reaction can reach dynamic equilibrium in a sealed container.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know that the characteristics of a reaction at dynamic equilibrium are:

items.label: list_item
items.text: the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate

items.label: list_item
items.text: the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

items.label: section_header
items.text: REVERSIBILITY AND DYNAMIC EQUILIBRIA

items.label: section_header
items.text: DEHYDRATION OF COPPER(II) SULFATE CRYSTALS

items.label: text
items.text: If you heat blue copper(Il) sulfate crystals gently, the blue crystals turn to a white powder and water is driven off. Heating causes the crystals to lose their water of crystallisation and white anhydrous copper(ll) sulfate is formed. 'Anhydrous'simply means'without water'.

items.label: formula
items.text: \begin{array} { c c c } \text {CuSO} _ { 4 } \cdot 5 H _ { 2 } O ( s ) \rightarrow \text {CuSO} _ { 4 } ( s ) + 5 H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) & \text {Heat is needed for this} \\ \text {blue} & \text {white} \end{array} \quad \text {reaction to occur}

items.label: text
items.text: If you add water to the white solid, it turns blue again; it also becomes very warm. See Figure 18.3 (page 192).

items.label: formula
items.text: \begin{smallmatrix} \text {CuSO} _ { 4 } ( s ) + 5 H _ { 2 } O ( i ) \rightarrow \text {CuSO} _ { 4 } \cdot 5 H _ { 2 } O ( s ) & \text {Heat is released from this} \\ \text {white} & \text {blue} \end{smallmatrix} \quad \text {reaction}

items.label: text
items.text: The original change has been exactly reversed. Even the heat that you put in originally has been given out again. This is called a reversible reaction and is indicated by a special arrow:

items.label: formula
items.text: C u S O _ { 4 } { \cdot } 5 H _ { 2 } O ( s ) \, \Longrightarrow \, C u S O _ { 4 } ( s ) + 5 H _ { 2 } O ( 1 )

items.label: section_header
items.text: HEATING AMMONIUM CHLORIDE

items.label: text
items.text: If you heat ammonium chloride, the white crystals disappear from the bottom of the tube and reappear further up. Heating ammonium chloride splits it into the colourless gases ammonia and hydrogen chloride.

items.label: section_header
items.text: TWO REVERSIBLE REACTIONS

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 21.1 Copper(ll) sulfate crystals are split into anhydrous copper(Il) sulfate and water on gentle heating.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand why a catalyst does not affect the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know the effect of changing either temperature or pressure on the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction:

items.label: list_item
items.text: an increase (or decrease) in temperature shifts the position of equilibrium in the direction of the endothermic (or exothermic) reaction

items.label: list_item
items.text: an increase (or decrease) in pressure shifts the position of equilibrium in the direction that produces fewer (or more) moles of gas.
